Which statement is TRUE about money in an insured savings account?

choices.text: It always grows faster than prices rise
It can be withdrawn with no limits of any kind at every bank in the country
It earns the same interest at every bank
Its value in dollars does not go down because of market changes

questions.correct_answer: Its value in dollars does not go down because of market changes
questions.feedback: Insured deposits do not lose dollars to market swings, though inflation can still reduce what the money buys.

questions.intro: The interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding. APY (annual percentage yield) shows what you actually earn in a year once interest is added to your balance and itself earns interest (compounding). Banks must show APY for savings, so use APY to compare accounts.
questions.question:
Two savings accounts show:
Bank A: interest rate 4.00%, compounded monthly; APY 4.07%
Bank B: APY 4.05%
Which number should Mo use to compare them fairly?

choices.text: The APY of each account
The interest rate of Bank A and the APY of Bank B
The interest rate of each, ignoring APY
Whichever number is printed larger in the ad

questions.correct_answer: The APY of each account
questions.feedback: APY includes compounding, so comparing APY to APY is fair. Bank A (4.07%) earns slightly more than Bank B (4.05%).

questions.intro: APY is the actual percent your money grows in one year, so one year of earnings ≈ balance × APY.
questions.question: An account has an APY of 4.07%. About how much will $2,000 earn in one year if the rate stays the same and nothing is withdrawn?

misconceptions.D: Gives the balance, not the interest

questions.intro: APY (annual percentage yield) is the percent your money actually grows in one year. The stated interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding.
questions.question: Why is APY usually a little higher than the stated interest rate?

choices.text: Interest that is added during the year also earns interest
Banks add a bonus to every account
APY includes extra deposits you plan to make later in the year
APY is the rate before taxes are added

questions.correct_answer: Interest that is added during the year also earns interest
questions.feedback: With compounding, earlier interest earns interest too, so the yearly yield is above the stated rate.

questions.intro: Most savings accounts have variable rates: the bank can raise or lower them, often when market interest rates change. A certificate of deposit usually locks a rate for its term.
questions.question: A savings rate is "variable." What does that mean?

choices.text: The rate is fixed until the account is closed
The rate depends on how many times you log in
The rate is negative in some months
The bank can change the rate over time

questions.correct_answer: The bank can change the rate over time
questions.feedback: Variable means the bank may change it; past or advertised rates are not promises.

questions.question: An ad shows "5.00% APY*", and the fine print says "*on balances up to $1,000; 0.50% APY on the amount above $1,000." Sara deposits $5,000. About how much interest will she earn in one year?

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: The $250,000 limit applies per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Money at two different banks is insured separately. (Two "brands" of the same bank are one bank for insurance purposes.)
questions.question: Marcus has $200,000 in an individual account at Bank A and $200,000 in an individual account at Bank B. Both banks are FDIC insured and separate. How much of his money is insured?

misconceptions.C: Applies one limit across different banks
misconceptions.A: Thinks large balances are never insured

questions.feedback: Each bank insures his $200,000 individually: $400,000 total.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Joint accounts are a separate ownership category from individual accounts. Each co-owner's share of joint accounts at one bank is insured up to $250,000.
questions.question: Sam and Pat own a joint account with $500,000 at one insured bank. Joint accounts are insured up to $250,000 per co-owner. How much is insured?

misconceptions.B: Applies one limit to the whole joint account

questions.feedback: Two co-owners × $250,000 = $500,000 of coverage, which covers the whole balance.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.question: Which product is covered by FDIC insurance when bought at an insured bank?

choices.text: A 12-month certificate of deposit
Shares of an index fund
A cryptocurrency purchase
The contents of a safe deposit box

questions.correct_answer: A 12-month certificate of deposit

misconceptions.B: Thinks funds sold at banks are insured
misconceptions.C: Thinks crypto at a bank is insured

questions.feedback: CDs are deposits. Investments, crypto assets, and safe deposit box contents are not insured deposits.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.intro: Only deposits at FDIC-insured banks (or NCUA-insured credit unions) are covered by deposit insurance. The FDIC warns consumers about companies that misrepresent their products as FDIC insured.
questions.question: A website for a company that sells crypto says, "Your funds are safe — like a bank." What should a careful saver conclude?

choices.text: The funds must be FDIC insured
The company is a federally chartered bank
The NCUA insures every crypto platform that operates in the United States
That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured

questions.correct_answer: That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured

misconceptions.A: Treats a comparison as a guarantee

questions.feedback: Comparisons to banks are not insurance. Check the FDIC's BankFind tool to see if an institution is an insured bank, and remember crypto assets are not deposits.

questions.section_skill: Deposit insurance limits and ownership categories
questions.question: Ella has $260,000 in one individual account at an insured bank and wants all of it insured. Which change would accomplish that most directly?

choices.text: Split it into two individual accounts at the same bank
Ask the bank to raise her personal limit
Withdraw the extra $10,000 and invest it in stocks for added safety
Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank

questions.correct_answer: Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank

misconceptions.A: Thinks multiple accounts in one category add coverage

questions.feedback: Coverage is per bank per category. Two individual accounts at the same bank share one $250,000 limit; a second bank adds coverage.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: A check is a written order telling your bank to pay someone from your account. You write the date, the payee (who gets paid), the amount in numbers, the amount in words with cents as a fraction of 100, and your signature. The words are the legal amount if the two differ.
questions.question: Nora writes a check for $1,254.07. How should she write the amount in words on the check?

choices.text: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars
One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 7/10 dollars
Twelve hundred fifty-four point zero seven
One thousand two hundred forty-five and 07/100 dollars

questions.correct_answer: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars

misconceptions.C: Uses "point" instead of the cents fraction

questions.feedback: $1,254.07 is written "One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars."

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: To deposit or cash a check made out to you, you "endorse" it by signing the back. Adding "For deposit only" (a restrictive endorsement) means the check can only be deposited, which protects it if it is lost. For mobile deposit, banks often require "For mobile deposit only" too.
questions.question: Ben receives a paycheck made out to him and wants to deposit it at an ATM. What should he write on the back?

choices.text: Nothing; endorsing a check is optional
His PIN, so the ATM can verify him
His account balance, so the bank can update it
His signature and "For deposit only"

questions.correct_answer: His signature and "For deposit only"

misconceptions.B: Writes sensitive data on a check
misconceptions.C: Thinks the balance goes on the check

questions.feedback: Signing with "For deposit only" endorses the check and limits it to being deposited.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Peer-to-peer (P2P) payment apps move money quickly between people. Money you send yourself, even to a scammer, is usually treated as authorized and is often hard to get back. Federal error protections focus on transfers you did not authorize. Use P2P apps mainly with people you know and trust.
questions.question: Mia sends $60 through a payment app to someone selling concert tickets online. The tickets never arrive. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse
The app must refund every payment that goes wrong
Her bank will reverse the payment automatically within one business day
The seller must legally deliver the tickets

questions.correct_answer: Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse

misconceptions.D: Thinks the law forces a scammer to deliver

questions.feedback: Because Mia authorized the payment, getting it back depends on the app's or bank's voluntary policies. Protections are stronger for unauthorized transfers.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.intro: Mobile check deposit lets you photograph a signed check in your bank's app. The bank may hold part of the money for a few days. Keep the paper check until the deposit is final, then destroy it securely so it cannot be deposited twice or misused.
questions.question: After depositing a check with his phone, what should Kai do with the paper check?

choices.text: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it
Deposit the same check again at the bank to be safe
Throw it in the trash right after taking the photo
Give it back to the person who wrote it

questions.correct_answer: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it

misconceptions.C: Discards it before the deposit is confirmed

questions.feedback: Keep it until the funds are final in case the bank needs it, then shred it.

questions.section_skill: Choose and use payment methods safely: checks, electronic transfers, and payment apps
questions.question: Zara's landlord asks for rent in a way that leaves a record of payment. Which method fits BEST?

choices.text: Cash handed over without a receipt
A gift card code sent by text
A wire transfer to an account number she has never verified
A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account

questions.correct_answer: A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account
questions.feedback: Checks and bank transfers leave records Zara can use as proof of payment.

questions.intro: Common ways to pay: cash; debit cards and checks (from your account); electronic transfers such as online bill pay and automatic payments (from your account, electronically); credit cards (borrowed money); and prepaid or gift cards (money loaded in advance).
questions.question: Which payment method moves money directly from your bank account electronically on a date you set?

choices.text: An online bill payment or automatic transfer
A paper check that the store mails to you each month
A credit card
A store gift card

questions.correct_answer: An online bill payment or automatic transfer

misconceptions.C: Confuses borrowing with paying from your account
misconceptions.D: Confuses prepaid value with an account payment

questions.feedback: Online bill pay and automatic payments take money from your account electronically.

questions.intro: A payment record proves you paid. Bank statements, cleared checks, and confirmation numbers are records. Cash leaves no record unless you get a receipt.
questions.question: Which method gives the LEAST proof that you paid?

choices.text: A check that the bank later shows as cleared
A debit card purchase listed on the statement
An online bill payment with a confirmation number
Cash with no receipt

questions.correct_answer: Cash with no receipt

misconceptions.A: A cleared check is a record

questions.feedback: Cash without a receipt leaves no proof of payment.

questions.intro: A prepaid or gift card holds a set amount of money. Each purchase is subtracted until the card reaches $0.
questions.question: A gift card loaded with $50 is used to buy a $12 item. What is left on the card?

misconceptions.C: Thinks the card balance does not change
misconceptions.A: Confuses the price with what is left

questions.question: Who is the "payee" on a check?

choices.text: The account holder who signs and writes the check
The bank that prints the check
The cashier who accepts the check
The person or business that receives the money

questions.correct_answer: The person or business that receives the money

misconceptions.A: Confuses payee with the account holder

questions.feedback: The payee is named on the "Pay to the order of" line.

questions.question: Which situation makes a payment app MOST risky to use?

choices.text: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
Splitting a dinner bill with a close friend
Paying a family member back for groceries
Sending rent money to a roommate you have lived with for a year

questions.correct_answer: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
questions.feedback: Paying strangers in advance is how many P2P scams work, because payments are hard to reverse.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A wire transfer moves money between banks quickly, often the same day, and is generally final once sent. ACH transfers (used for direct deposit and online bill pay) move money between bank accounts more slowly and have some ways to return errors. Scammers often ask for wires because they are fast and hard to reverse.
questions.question: Which payment is generally the hardest to reverse once sent?

choices.text: A wire transfer
A credit card purchase
A check that has not been cashed yet
A debit card purchase you did not authorize

questions.correct_answer: A wire transfer

misconceptions.C: A stop payment may be possible

questions.feedback: Wires are fast and generally final, which is why scammers prefer them.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so a real one is very reliable. But fake cashier's checks are common. The bank may make the money available before discovering the check is fake; when it bounces, you owe the bank the full amount.
questions.question: A buyer sends Liam a cashier's check for $1,500 for a $500 phone and asks him to wire back the extra $1,000. What is most likely happening?

choices.text: A generous buyer making an honest mistake
A normal practice for cashier's checks
A bank error that the bank will cover
A fake-check scam

questions.correct_answer: A fake-check scam

misconceptions.A: Ignores the classic overpayment scam pattern
misconceptions.C: Thinks the bank absorbs fraud losses

questions.feedback: Overpayment with a request to send money back is a classic fake-check scam. Liam would owe the bank when the check bounces.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: The ACH (Automated Clearing House) network moves money electronically between bank accounts in batches. It is cheaper and slower than a wire transfer.
questions.question: Which is a typical use of an ACH transfer?

choices.text: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
Buying groceries with cash
Paying a bill with a paper money order bought at a store
Swiping a credit card at a store

questions.correct_answer: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
questions.feedback: Direct deposit and many automatic bill payments use the ACH network.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Criminals hack or fake emails and send new "updated" wire instructions so money goes to their account. Because wires are hard to reverse, verify instructions through a trusted phone number, not one in the suspicious email.
questions.question: Before wiring money for a home or apartment deposit, what is the safest step?

choices.text: Use the instructions in the most recent email, even if they changed
Wire the money quickly so you do not lose the apartment
Ask the sender to text you the account number again
Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

questions.correct_answer: Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions

misconceptions.C: Uses the same possibly hacked channel

questions.feedback: Independent verification defeats changed-instructions scams.

questions.section_skill: Wires, ACH transfers, and official checks
questions.intro: Until a check is paid by your bank, you can ask the bank not to pay it. Banks usually charge a fee for this service, and it does not work on a check that has already cleared.
questions.question: Ruth wrote a check and then learned it was lost in the mail before it was cashed. What service could stop it?

choices.text: A wire recall, which works on all checks
Reporting the check to the IRS
Writing a second check for the same amount
A stop payment order through her bank

questions.correct_answer: A stop payment order through her bank
questions.feedback: A stop payment order tells the bank not to pay that check, if it has not already cleared.

questions.intro: A common scam claims you received money "by mistake" and asks you to send it back. Sometimes the original payment was made with stolen information and is later reversed, leaving you with the loss. Verify inside your own app or bank, never through a link or message.
questions.question: Someone texts Ava: "I sent you $200 by mistake — please send it back!" Her app shows no new money in her account. What should she do?

choices.text: Check her own account directly and send nothing
Send $200 back right away to be polite
Reply with her bank login so they can fix it
Send $100 as a compromise

questions.correct_answer: Check her own account directly and send nothing

misconceptions.D: Still sends money to a scammer

questions.feedback: Without verified money in her own account, there is nothing to return. Even if money did arrive, contact the app's support rather than sending money.

questions.question: Which setting adds the most protection to a payment app?

choices.text: Sharing your login with a parent and a friend so they can watch for fraud
Using the same password as your email
Turning off notifications
Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app

questions.correct_answer: Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app
questions.feedback: Multi-factor authentication and an app passcode make unauthorized access much harder.

questions.intro: Real banks and payment apps do not ask you to move money to a "safe account" to protect it. Imposters pretend to be bank staff, tech support, or government officials and create urgency.
questions.question: A "customer support" caller says your payment app is hacked and asks you to send your balance to a "safe account." What is this?

choices.text: An imposter scam
A standard security procedure
A government requirement
A way to earn extra interest

questions.correct_answer: An imposter scam

misconceptions.B: Real companies do not ask this

questions.feedback: Any request to move money to protect it is a red flag for an imposter scam. Hang up and call the official number.

questions.question: Which payment is generally protected under federal error rules (Regulation E)?

choices.text: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
A payment you chose to send to an online seller who never shipped
A payment you sent to the wrong person after typing their name
Money you lost gambling with an app

questions.correct_answer: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission

questions.question: Jess takes home $2,800 a month. Using the 50/30/20 guideline (50% needs, 30% wants, 20% saving and debt payoff), how much goes to saving and extra debt payments?

questions.section_skill: Use percentages to plan and evaluate a budget
questions.intro: To find what percent one amount is of another: part ÷ whole × 100.
questions.question: Jess pays $900 rent from $2,800 take-home pay. What percent of her take-home pay is rent (nearest tenth of a percent)?

questions.section_skill: Use percentages to plan and evaluate a budget
questions.question: Ian wants his car costs to be no more than 15% of his $2,400 take-home pay. What is the most he should spend per month on his car?

questions.section_skill: Use percentages to plan and evaluate a budget
questions.question: Jess lives in a high-rent city where needs take 62% of her pay. What is the best way to use the 50/30/20 guideline (50% needs, 30% wants, 20% saving)?

choices.text: As a legal limit she must follow exactly
By ignoring it, since budgets do not use percents
As a starting point, adjusting the shares to fit her costs
By moving her rent into the "wants" share

questions.correct_answer: As a starting point, adjusting the shares to fit her costs
questions.feedback: Guidelines are starting points. With 62% for needs, she might plan 62/18/20 and look for ways to lower needs over time.

questions.intro: Percent means "per hundred." 20% of income means $20 of every $100 earned.
questions.question: What does "20% of income goes to savings" mean?

choices.text: 20 dollars of every month go to savings
Savings are 20 times income
Savings get the first 20 dollars only
20 of every 100 dollars of income go to savings

questions.correct_answer: 20 of every 100 dollars of income go to savings

misconceptions.A: Reads percent as a dollar amount
misconceptions.C: Reads percent as a fixed amount

questions.question: What is 30% of $1,000?

questions.intro: Percent of the whole = part ÷ whole × 100.
questions.question: $250 of a $1,000 paycheck goes to rent. What percent is that?

misconceptions.D: Uses the dollar amount as a percent

questions.question: A budget uses 50%, 30%, and 20%. What do the percents add up to?
questions.feedback: 50 + 30 + 20 = 100%: the whole income.

questions.question: If needs are 50% of $2,000, what dollar amount is that?

questions.intro: When you know the part and the percent, find the whole: whole = part ÷ percent (as a decimal).
questions.question: Rent for an apartment is $1,050. Ana wants rent to be no more than 30% of her take-home pay. What monthly take-home pay does she need?
Leo wants to save $300 a month, which he wants to be 15% of take-home pay. What take-home pay does this require?
Leo's take-home pay is $1,800, and he spends $1,170 on needs. What percent is that?
Leo's needs are 65%. To reach 20% savings, what is the most he can spend on wants?

misconceptions.D: Uses all the remainder for wants

questions.question: With $1,800 take-home pay and 15% for wants, how many dollars is that?

questions.intro: A variance is the difference between what you planned and what actually happened. Reviewing variances each month shows which parts of the plan need work.
questions.question: Planned: groceries $300. Actual: $345. What is the variance, and is it over or under budget?

choices.text: $45 under budget
$45 over budget
$645 over budget
$15 over budget

questions.correct_answer: $45 over budget
questions.feedback: $345 − $300 = $45 more than planned.

questions.question: What percent over budget is $345 compared with a $300 plan?

misconceptions.A: Divides by actual instead of planned
misconceptions.D: Gives actual as a percent of planned

questions.question: Gas was budgeted at $120 and came in at $96. What is the variance?

choices.text: $24 over budget
$216 under budget
$96 under budget
$24 under budget

questions.correct_answer: $24 under budget
questions.feedback: $120 − $96 = $24 less than planned.

questions.question: Ray budgeted $120 for gas but spent only $96, leaving $24. Which response best supports a savings goal?

choices.text: Spend it on a want right away because it was "free"
Leave it unassigned so it is spent on something later
Move the $24 into savings
Lower next month's gas budget to $0

questions.correct_answer: Move the $24 into savings
questions.feedback: Assigning surpluses to goals keeps the budget working.

questions.question: Over 3 months, eating out was $40, $120, and $35 over budget. Which conclusion is BEST?

choices.text: One unusual month; review it, but the plan is close
The budget is perfect and needs no review
The budget should triple the eating-out line
Budgets do not work for eating out

questions.correct_answer: One unusual month; review it, but the plan is close
questions.feedback: Look for patterns, not single months; one large month may be a special event.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: Some expenses come once or twice a year: car registration, insurance premiums, school fees, gifts. A sinking fund saves a little each month for a known future expense, so the full amount is ready when it is due. Monthly amount = total ÷ months until due.
questions.question: Cara's car registration costs $180 once a year. How much should she set aside each month so the money is ready?

misconceptions.D: Plans to pay the whole amount in one month

questions.feedback: $180 ÷ 12 = $15 per month.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: A sinking fund is for a KNOWN future cost with a known date. An emergency fund is for UNKNOWN surprises, such as a job loss or a sudden repair.
questions.question: Which is a sinking fund?

choices.text: Money spent on groceries each week of the month
An emergency fund for surprises you cannot predict
Saving $50 a month for car insurance due every six months
A loan used to pay a bill that is already past due

questions.correct_answer: Saving $50 a month for car insurance due every six months
questions.feedback: Saving monthly for a known, scheduled bill is a sinking fund.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.question: Cara's yearly irregular costs: registration $180, car insurance $960, and holiday gifts $300. How much should she set aside each month in total?

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.intro: When the due date is less than a year away, divide by the months remaining, not by 12.
questions.question: It is March. Holiday gifts ($600) will be bought in November, 8 months away. How much should Ben save each month?

misconceptions.D: Saves it all in one month

questions.feedback: $600 ÷ 8 = $75 per month.

questions.section_skill: Plan for periodic and irregular expenses with monthly set-asides
questions.question: Why do budgets that ignore irregular expenses often fail?

choices.text: Irregular expenses are illegal to budget for
Large, predictable bills arrive with no money set aside
Irregular expenses are always paid by employers
Banks automatically pay irregular bills for free

questions.correct_answer: Large, predictable bills arrive with no money set aside
questions.feedback: Spreading known costs across months prevents "surprise" bills that were predictable.

questions.intro: To turn a yearly amount into a monthly amount, divide by 12. To turn a monthly amount into a yearly amount, multiply by 12.
questions.question: A yearly fee is $240. What is the monthly equivalent?
A $35 monthly subscription costs how much per year?

questions.intro: For a bill due every few months, divide by the number of months between bills.
questions.question: A bill of $300 is due every 6 months. How much is that per month?
questions.feedback: $300 ÷ 6 = $50 per month.

questions.question: Which expense is MOST likely to be paid once a year?

choices.text: A weekly grocery trip
A monthly phone bill
A daily bus fare
A car registration renewal

questions.correct_answer: A car registration renewal
questions.feedback: Registrations, many insurance policies, and some memberships are yearly.

questions.question: A quarterly bill is due every 3 months. How many times a year is it paid?

misconceptions.B: Confuses months between bills with bills per year

questions.feedback: 12 months ÷ 3 = 4 payments per year.

questions.intro: When income varies (tips, commissions, gig work, seasonal jobs), budgeting on a low but realistic month keeps needs covered. Extra income in good months goes to savings or a "buffer" that carries you through slow months.
questions.question: Mo's monthly income over the last six months: $1,800, $2,600, $1,500, $2,200, $1,900, $2,400. Which amount is the safest base for his budget?

misconceptions.B: Uses the average, which leaves no cushion in low months

questions.feedback: Planning on the lowest recent month ($1,500) keeps needs covered in slow months.

questions.question: Mo's monthly income over six months: $1,800, $2,600, $1,500, $2,200, $1,900, $2,400. What is his average monthly income?

choices.text: About $2,067

questions.correct_answer: About $2,067

misconceptions.B: Uses the middle of the range

questions.question: Mo budgets $1,500 a month and saves any income above that in a buffer account. In a $2,600 month, how much goes to his buffer account?
Mo budgets $1,500 a month and keeps extra income from good months in a buffer account. In a $1,200 month, what should he do?

choices.text: Put $300 on a credit card
Draw $300 from his buffer account
Skip rent this month
Raise his budget to $2,600

questions.correct_answer: Draw $300 from his buffer account
questions.feedback: The buffer exists to cover low months: $1,500 − $1,200 = $300.

questions.intro: Some workers with uneven income deposit all earnings into one account and transfer a fixed amount to their spending account each month, like a salary.
questions.question: Which practice makes uneven income easier to manage?

choices.text: Spending each paycheck as soon as it arrives
Budgeting from your single best month
Paying yourself a steady "salary" from a holding account
Avoiding any record of income

questions.correct_answer: Paying yourself a steady "salary" from a holding account
questions.feedback: A steady transfer smooths uneven income into predictable spending money.

questions.intro: Many services offer a discount for paying a year at once. Compare by finding the yearly cost of the monthly plan. But a yearly plan only saves money if you would have kept the service all year.
questions.question: A streaming service costs $15.99 per month or $159.99 per year. How much does the yearly plan save compared with paying monthly for 12 months?

misconceptions.D: Subtracts the monthly price from the yearly price
misconceptions.B: Subtracts dollar amounts digit by digit

questions.question: Gina usually cancels streaming services after about 6 months. For her, which plan is cheaper: 6 months at $15.99, or the $159.99 yearly plan?

choices.text: Yearly: $159.99
They cost the same
Monthly: $191.88
Monthly: about $95.94

questions.correct_answer: Monthly: about $95.94

misconceptions.A: Assumes she keeps it all year

questions.question: A gym offers $40 per month with no contract, or $360 for a full year paid up front. After how many months does the yearly plan become the better deal?

choices.text: More than 9 months
More than 4 months
More than 12 months
More than 3 months

questions.correct_answer: More than 9 months

misconceptions.C: Thinks the yearly plan never wins

questions.feedback: $360 ÷ $40 = 9. If she uses the gym more than 9 months, the yearly plan saves money.

questions.question: Which is a risk of a large annual prepayment?

choices.text: The price can never change
Paying for months you may not use
You get a discount
Fewer bills to track

questions.correct_answer: Paying for months you may not use
questions.feedback: Prepaying locks money into a service you might stop using; check the refund policy.

questions.question: A $12.99 monthly subscription renews automatically. Over 3 years, how much does it cost if never cancelled?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: A unit price is the price per unit, such as per ounce or per item: unit price = price ÷ quantity. Comparing unit prices shows which size is the better value. (A lower unit price helps only if you will use the larger amount before it spoils.)
questions.question: A 12-ounce box of cereal costs $3.60. A 20-ounce box costs $5.40. Which is the better buy per ounce?

choices.text: The 20-ounce box: $0.27 per ounce
The 12-ounce box: $0.30 per ounce
The 12-ounce box, because it costs less
The 20-ounce box: $0.30 per ounce

questions.correct_answer: The 20-ounce box: $0.27 per ounce

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: A discount is a percent taken off the price. Discount = price × rate. Sale price = price − discount, or price × (1 − rate).
questions.question: A $64 backpack is 25% off. What is the sale price?

misconceptions.A: Gives the discount, not the sale price

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: Sales tax is calculated by multiplying the taxable price by the tax rate. Total cost = price + tax, or price × (1 + rate). Rates differ by state and sometimes by city, and some items are exempt.
questions.question: A taxable purchase costs $80. The sales tax rate is 6.5%. What is the TOTAL cost?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: When a discount and a tax both apply, the discount is taken first, and tax is then figured on the sale price.
questions.question: A $120 jacket is 30% off, and the 6.5% sales tax is applied to the sale price. What is the total cost?

misconceptions.D: Applies tax to the original price and adds it to the sale price

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Compare prices using unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: A store offers "Buy one, get one 50% off" on $20 shirts. If Tom buys two, what percent does he save on the pair?

misconceptions.A: Uses the dollar amount as a percent

questions.feedback: Two shirts: $20 + $10 = $30 instead of $40. Savings $10 ÷ $40 = 25%.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: A discount lowers the price: sale price = original price − discount.
questions.question: A $50 item has a $10 discount. What is the sale price?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: Sales tax raises the total: total = price + tax.
questions.question: The tax on a $40 item is $2.60. What is the total?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: Which word describes the percent taken OFF a price?

choices.text: Tax
Total
Interest
Discount

questions.correct_answer: Discount

misconceptions.C: Interest is a borrowing or saving cost

questions.feedback: A discount reduces the price.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: 10% of an amount is the amount divided by 10.
questions.question: What is 10% of $35?

misconceptions.C: Gives the price after the discount

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: Which comparison tells you the better buy between two package sizes?

choices.text: Which package is larger
Which package is cheaper in total
Price per ounce of each package
Which package has brighter colors

questions.correct_answer: Price per ounce of each package

misconceptions.A: Size alone does not give value

questions.feedback: Unit price compares value across sizes.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.intro: When discounts "stack," each is applied to the price left after the previous one. Two discounts of 20% and 10% do not equal 30% off.
questions.question: A $100 coat is 20% off, with an extra 10% off the sale price at checkout. What is the final price before tax?

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: What single percent discount is the same as 20% off followed by 10% off?

misconceptions.A: Multiplies the percents as whole numbers

questions.feedback: Final price is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72 of the original, so the discount is 28%.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: A $5-off coupon and a 15% discount can be used in either order on a $40 purchase. Which order gives the lower price?

choices.text: $5 first, then 15% off: $29.75
15% first, then $5 off: $29.00
Both orders give $29.00
15% first, then $5 off: $34.00

questions.correct_answer: 15% first, then $5 off: $29.00

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: An ad says "Up to 70% off!" What does this usually mean?

choices.text: Only some items are 70% off; many are discounted less
Every item is 70% off
Every item is at least 70% off
The store adds 70% to prices

questions.correct_answer: Only some items are 70% off; many are discounted less
questions.feedback: "Up to" sets the maximum discount, not the typical one.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.question: An item's price was $80 last week and is now "on sale" for $80 after being raised to $100 and marked 20% off. What happened?

choices.text: Tom saves $20 compared with last week
Tom saves 20% compared with last week
The "sale" price is the same as last week's price
The price went down by $100

questions.correct_answer: The "sale" price is the same as last week's price
questions.feedback: $100 × 0.80 = $80, the same as before. Compare with past prices, not just the "was" price.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.intro: Compare total cost: price + shipping + fees + tax. A lower sticker price can cost more in total.
questions.question: Store A sells headphones for $59 plus $8 shipping. Store B sells them for $64 with free shipping. Which costs less, and by how much?

choices.text: Store A, by $5
Store B, by $5
They cost the same
Store B, by $3

questions.correct_answer: Store B, by $3

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.question: A store offers free shipping on orders of $50 or more. Jen's cart totals $42, and shipping is $7. She adds a $10 item she does not need. What did that cost her compared with paying shipping?

choices.text: $3 more
$7 less
$10 less
$17 more

questions.correct_answer: $3 more
questions.feedback: Paying shipping: $49. Adding the item: $52. She spends $3 more, on something she does not need.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.intro: Sales tax rules are set by each state. Some items, such as groceries, clothing, or medicine, may be exempt. Always check your own state's rules.
questions.question: In New Jersey, most clothing and most grocery food are exempt from sales tax, and the general rate is 6.625%. What is the tax on a $40 shirt and a $40 desk lamp bought together?
questions.feedback: The shirt is exempt; the lamp is taxable: $40 × 0.06625 = $2.65.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.question: Which purchase decision considers the total cost of owning an item?

choices.text: Choosing the printer with the lowest sticker price only
Choosing the printer with the most colors on the box
Comparing printers by price plus yearly ink costs
Choosing the printer the store displays first

questions.correct_answer: Comparing printers by price plus yearly ink costs
questions.feedback: Ongoing costs (ink, fuel, subscriptions, repairs) can matter more than the purchase price.

questions.set_title: Smart shopping: unit prices, discounts, and sales tax
questions.section_skill: Total cost beyond the price tag
questions.question: Printer X costs $60 and $80 a year in ink. Printer Y costs $150 and $35 a year in ink. Over 3 years, which costs less in total?

choices.text: Printer X: $140 vs $185
Printer Y: $255 vs $300
Printer X: $60 vs $150
They cost the same over 3 years

questions.correct_answer: Printer Y: $255 vs $300

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Every spending choice has an opportunity cost: the next-best thing you give up. Thinking about what else money could do helps you choose deliberately rather than automatically.
questions.question: Kai has $200. He can buy a game console accessory or save toward a used bike. If he buys the accessory, what is the opportunity cost?

choices.text: The $200 price of the accessory itself, paid at the register
Nothing, because he still has the accessory
The sales tax on the accessory
The progress toward the bike that he gives up

questions.correct_answer: The progress toward the bike that he gives up

misconceptions.A: Confuses price with what is given up

questions.feedback: Choosing the accessory means giving up progress toward the bike, the next-best option.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Anchoring is relying too much on the first number you see. A high "original" price can make a sale price feel cheap, even when it is not a good deal compared with other options.
questions.question: A sign says "Was $200, now $120!" Mia feels the $120 price is a great deal, even though similar items cost $100 elsewhere. Which bias is at work?

choices.text: Sunk cost thinking about money already spent
Loss aversion about a past investment loss
The bandwagon effect from friends' choices
Anchoring on the "was" price

questions.correct_answer: Anchoring on the "was" price
questions.feedback: The $200 anchor makes $120 seem cheap; comparing with $100 elsewhere shows it is not.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered. The sunk cost fallacy is letting it drive a new decision. Good decisions compare the future benefits and costs of each option.
questions.question: Leo paid $60 for a concert ticket but feels sick on the day. He goes anyway "so the money isn't wasted." What is this called?

choices.text: Opportunity cost
The sunk cost fallacy
Anchoring
Comparison shopping

questions.correct_answer: The sunk cost fallacy
questions.feedback: The $60 is gone either way; the choice should depend on how he feels and what he gains now.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.intro: Present bias is valuing what we want now much more than what we want later. Impulse buying feeds on it. Adding a delay, such as a 24-hour rule or removing saved cards, gives the planning part of the brain time to weigh in.
questions.question: Ana often buys things online late at night and regrets them. Which strategy targets this habit directly?

choices.text: Save her card details on every site so checkout is faster
Turn on more shopping notifications
Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned
Shop only during sales events

questions.correct_answer: Wait 24 hours before buying anything not planned
questions.feedback: A waiting period interrupts impulse buying and lets her compare the purchase with her goals.

questions.section_skill: Use a decision process and recognize biases that lead to poor spending choices
questions.question: Which ordering follows a sound decision process?

choices.text: Set a goal, list options, compare, choose, review
Choose quickly, then find reasons to justify the choice later
List options, choose the most popular, skip review
Compare costs only after buying

questions.correct_answer: Set a goal, list options, compare, choose, review
questions.feedback: A deliberate process defines the goal and compares options before choosing, then reviews the result.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.intro: Every decision has alternatives (the options) and criteria (what matters to you, such as price, quality, or coverage). Good choices compare alternatives using your criteria.
questions.question: Sam is choosing a phone plan. What are "alternatives"?

choices.text: The different plans he could choose
The reasons he wants a phone
The phone he already owns
The bill he paid last month

questions.correct_answer: The different plans he could choose
questions.feedback: Alternatives are the options he is choosing among.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.intro: A criterion (plural: criteria) is a standard you use to judge options, such as cost, quality, or features that matter to you.
questions.question: Which is a CRITERION for choosing a phone plan?

choices.text: The store's background music
The salesperson's name
Monthly price
The plan's advertisement color

questions.correct_answer: Monthly price
questions.feedback: Price, data, and coverage are criteria that matter for the choice.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.question: Plan A: $35, 5 GB. Plan B: $45, unlimited. Sam uses about 3 GB a month. Which plan fits his criteria of low cost and enough data?

choices.text: Plan B, because unlimited always sounds better
Plan A
Neither, because both cost money
Plan B, because it costs more

questions.correct_answer: Plan A
questions.feedback: Plan A covers his 3 GB for $10 less per month.

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.question: Plan A costs $35 a month and Plan B costs $45 a month. What is the yearly savings from choosing Plan A?

questions.section_skill: Making a choice: alternatives and criteria
questions.question: After choosing, why review the decision a month later?

choices.text: Because contracts require monthly reviews
To find someone to blame
Because reviewing a purchase lowers its price later
To check whether the choice worked as expected

questions.correct_answer: To check whether the choice worked as expected
questions.feedback: Reviewing lets you learn and adjust future choices.

questions.intro: Scarcity and urgency messages ("only a few left," countdown timers) push quick decisions. Sometimes they are true, sometimes not. Slowing down protects your budget.
questions.question: A website shows "Only 2 left!" and a countdown timer. What is the intended effect?

choices.text: Helping the buyer compare options calmly
Lowering the price
Rushing the buyer before comparing options
Showing the store's full inventory honestly

questions.correct_answer: Rushing the buyer before comparing options
questions.feedback: Urgency cues are designed to cut comparison short.

questions.question: A "free trial" requires a card and converts to $14.99 a month unless cancelled. What should Nia do before signing up?

choices.text: Assume it will cancel itself automatically
Set a reminder to cancel before the trial ends
Use a friend's card instead
Ignore the terms, since the trial is advertised as free

questions.correct_answer: Set a reminder to cancel before the trial ends
questions.feedback: Free trials often become paid subscriptions automatically; a reminder prevents unwanted charges.

questions.question: A store's loyalty program gives 5% back in points. Raj spends $200 more than he planned to earn points. What did he gain compared with not overspending?

choices.text: He saved $10
He broke even
He saved $200
He spent $190 more, net of $10 in points

questions.correct_answer: He spent $190 more, net of $10 in points
questions.feedback: 5% of $200 = $10 in points, but he spent $200 extra: a net cost of $190.

questions.intro: "Dark patterns" are design tricks that steer people into choices they did not intend, such as hidden fees, pre-checked add-ons, or hard-to-find cancellation steps.
questions.question: Which design choice is a "dark pattern" that makes spending easier than intended?

choices.text: Making cancellation much harder than signing up
Showing the total price before checkout
Listing all fees clearly up front
Offering a clear "cancel" button

questions.correct_answer: Making cancellation much harder than signing up
questions.feedback: Easy sign-up and hard cancellation is a common dark pattern.

questions.question: At checkout, a $4.99 "protection plan" box is already checked on Ben's $25 order. What should he do?

choices.text: Leave it, since stores must check what customers need
Uncheck it unless he decided he wants it
Pay it, because it is under $5
Buy two to be safe

questions.correct_answer: Uncheck it unless he decided he wants it

misconceptions.C: Ignores that it is 20% of the order

questions.feedback: Pre-checked add-ons rely on default bias; $4.99 is about 20% of a $25 order.

questions.intro: Influencers are often paid to promote products and may earn money from each sale. Federal rules require disclosure of these relationships, but the incentive still shapes the message.
questions.question: An influencer promotes a product with a discount code. Which fact matters MOST?

choices.text: The influencer may be paid for each sale
The influencer has many followers
The video looks professional and well produced
The product is popular this week

questions.correct_answer: The influencer may be paid for each sale
questions.feedback: A paid relationship is a reason to compare reviews and prices independently.

questions.question: Friends spend $80 on a dinner out each weekend. Tara's budget allows $30. Which choice best balances friendship and her budget?

choices.text: Join every time and put the extra on a credit card
Skip all social events forever
Join for a lower-cost part or suggest a cheaper place
Cut her rent payment to afford it

questions.correct_answer: Join for a lower-cost part or suggest a cheaper place
questions.feedback: Adapting the plan keeps both the friendships and the budget.

questions.question: Seeing friends' purchases online makes Eli feel he must buy similar things. What is this effect sometimes called?

choices.text: Compound interest
Diversification

questions.intro: Collateral is property a borrower pledges to a lender. A secured loan is backed by collateral (a car for an auto loan, a home for a mortgage); if the borrower does not repay, the lender can take it. An unsecured loan has no collateral, so lenders usually charge more.
questions.question: Which loan is SECURED?

choices.text: A credit card with no collateral
An auto loan where the lender can repossess the car
A personal loan approved based only on the borrower's income
A student loan with no collateral

questions.correct_answer: An auto loan where the lender can repossess the car
questions.feedback: The car is collateral for an auto loan, so it is secured.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral
questions.section_skill: Explain the parts of a loan and compare secured and unsecured borrowing
questions.intro: Interest rates reflect risk. When a lender cannot take property to recover a loan, it faces more risk of loss and usually charges a higher rate.
questions.question: Why do unsecured loans usually have HIGHER interest rates than secured loans?

choices.text: Unsecured loans are always larger
Secured loans are not regulated, so they can charge anything
The lender has no collateral to take if unpaid
Unsecured lenders must pay extra taxes

questions.correct_answer: The lender has no collateral to take if unpaid
questions.feedback: More risk for the lender means a higher rate.

questions.set_title: Borrowing basics: principal, interest, term, and collateral

A loan for a vacation that will be paid off over five years
A cash advance to buy concert tickets
A loan to cover gambling losses

questions.correct_answer: A modest loan for training that raises future earnings

misconceptions.B: Long-term debt for a short-term want
misconceptions.D: Debt that does not create value

questions.feedback: Borrowing that builds income or lasting value can be worthwhile; borrowing for short-lived wants usually costs more than it is worth.

She automatically owns the car

questions.section_skill: Interpret APR and convert it to monthly and daily periodic rates
questions.intro: APR (annual percentage rate) is the yearly cost of credit, including the interest rate and certain fees, expressed as a percent. Lenders often charge interest each month using a periodic rate: monthly periodic rate = APR ÷ 12.

misconceptions.D: Confuses APR with a daily rate

questions.section_skill: APR versus APY and effective cost

APR leaves out compounding, so it looks lower

APR is used only for savings

questions.feedback: The effective cost with compounding is higher than the stated APR.

Lower
Exactly 24%

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

misconceptions.D: Treats the extra payment as interest saved

questions.feedback: $50 × 0.005 = $0.25 less interest in month 2, and similar savings every month after.

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: Extra payments on principal reduce the balance faster than the schedule, so later payments carry less interest.
questions.question: On an amortizing loan with no prepayment penalty, what happens to the loan when extra principal is paid each month?

choices.text: The required monthly payment goes up automatically
It is paid off sooner, and total interest falls
The interest rate rises
Nothing changes

questions.correct_answer: It is paid off sooner, and total interest falls
questions.feedback: Lower balance → less interest → earlier payoff.

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: Some lenders apply extra money to future payments unless told otherwise. Telling them to apply it to principal reduces the balance right away.
questions.question: When making an extra payment, what instruction should a borrower give the lender?

choices.text: Apply it to next month's interest only
Hold it as a credit for fees
Refund it at the end of the year
Apply the extra amount to principal

questions.correct_answer: Apply the extra amount to principal
questions.feedback: Directing it to principal ensures the balance and future interest fall.

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.question: Dev rounds his $193.33 payment up to $200 each month. How much extra principal does he pay in a year?

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: The earlier principal is reduced, the more months of interest are avoided.
questions.question: Which statement about extra payments is TRUE for most amortizing loans with no prepayment penalty?

choices.text: Extra payments only help in the final year
Extra dollars paid early save more than late ones
Extra payments increase the total interest paid on the loan
Extra payments are not allowed

questions.correct_answer: Extra dollars paid early save more than late ones
questions.feedback: Early extra principal avoids interest for many more months.

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: Each row of an amortization schedule shows the payment, its interest part, its principal part, and the balance after the payment.
questions.question: Row 12 of a schedule shows: payment $193.33, interest $44.22, principal $149.11, balance $8,694.98. How much of payment 12 reduced the debt?
questions.feedback: The principal part, $149.11, reduced the debt.

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: Balance before payment = balance after payment + principal part.
questions.question: A schedule row shows: interest $44.22, principal $149.11, balance $8,694.98 after the payment. What was the balance before that payment?

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: Over the full life of a loan, the principal parts of all payments add up to the amount borrowed.
questions.question: In a 60-payment schedule for $10,000 at 6% APR, the total of the interest column is about $1,599.80. What is the total of the principal column?
questions.feedback: The principal parts repay exactly the amount borrowed.

questions.set_title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
questions.intro: "Front-loaded" means more of something comes at the beginning.
questions.question: Which schedule feature shows that a loan is "front-loaded" with interest?

choices.text: Interest parts are largest in the first payments
The balance rises each month
Every payment has an equal amount of interest in it
The last payment is all interest
