questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Calculate and compare the true cost of high-cost credit and identify safer alternatives
questions.intro: Payday loans are small, short-term loans, often due on your next payday, with a flat fee. Converting the fee to an APR shows the true yearly cost: APR = (fee ÷ amount borrowed) × (365 ÷ days) × 100.
questions.question: A payday lender charges a $45 fee to borrow $300 for 14 days. What is the APR (nearest whole percent)?

misconceptions.A: Gives the fee as a percent of the loan for two weeks
misconceptions.C: Uses the fee as a percent
misconceptions.B: Counts the number of two-week periods

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Calculate and compare the true cost of high-cost credit and identify safer alternatives
questions.intro: A rollover (or renewal) pays only the fee and extends the loan, so the original amount is still owed. Repeated rollovers can cost more than the original loan.
questions.question: Instead of repaying, Kim "rolls over" a $300 payday loan four times, paying a $45 fee each time. How much has she paid in fees, and how much does she still owe?

choices.text: $45 in fees; owes nothing
$180 in fees; owes nothing
$180 in fees; still owes $300
$300 in fees; owes $45

questions.correct_answer: $180 in fees; still owes $300

misconceptions.A: Thinks one fee repays the loan

questions.feedback: 4 × $45 = $180 in fees, and the $300 principal is still due.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Calculate and compare the true cost of high-cost credit and identify safer alternatives
questions.intro: Rent-to-own lets you use an item while making weekly or monthly payments; you own it only after all payments. The total paid is often far more than the store price.
questions.question: A rent-to-own store offers a TV for $25 a week for 78 weeks. The same TV sells for $600. How much more does rent-to-own cost?

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Calculate and compare the true cost of high-cost credit and identify safer alternatives
questions.intro: A car title loan is a short-term loan that uses your vehicle as collateral. Fees are high, and if you cannot repay, the lender can repossess the car you may need to get to work.
questions.question: A car title loan lends Ray $1,000 using his car as collateral, with a 25% monthly fee. What is the biggest risk?

choices.text: The fee will lower his car insurance
He could lose the car if he cannot repay
His credit score will automatically rise
The lender will pay off his car loan

questions.correct_answer: He could lose the car if he cannot repay
questions.feedback: The car is collateral; losing it can also cost him his job transportation.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Calculate and compare the true cost of high-cost credit and identify safer alternatives
questions.intro: Buy now, pay later plans let you split a purchase into a few installments, often with no interest if paid on time. Late fees can apply, several plans at once can be hard to track, and spending can creep up.
questions.question: Buy now, pay later (BNPL) splits a $200 purchase into 4 payments of $50 every two weeks with no interest. Jo misses two payments and is charged a $7 late fee each time. What does the purchase cost her?

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Fees as a cost of borrowing
questions.intro: Fees are part of the cost of borrowing, just like interest. Total repaid = amount borrowed + interest + fees.
questions.question: A lender charges a $20 fee to borrow $100 for one month. What is the cost of borrowing?

choices.text: $0, because it is a fee not interest

misconceptions.D: Thinks fees are not a cost

questions.feedback: The $20 fee is the cost of borrowing.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Fees as a cost of borrowing
questions.intro: Fee as a percent = fee ÷ amount borrowed × 100.
questions.question: The $20 fee on a $100 one-month loan is what percent of the amount borrowed?
questions.feedback: $20 ÷ $100 = 20% for one month.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Fees as a cost of borrowing
questions.intro: A simple yearly rate is the monthly rate × 12.
questions.question: If that 20% monthly cost continued all year, about what yearly rate would it be (simple)?

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Fees as a cost of borrowing
questions.intro: Credit unions, some banks, and employers offer small-dollar loans or paycheck advances at much lower cost than payday lenders. Asking a creditor for more time or using savings also avoids high fees.
questions.question: Which is a lower-cost alternative to a payday loan for a $200 emergency?

choices.text: A second payday loan to pay the first
A car title loan
A rent-to-own purchase
A small loan from a credit union

questions.correct_answer: A small loan from a credit union

misconceptions.B: High cost and risk to the car

questions.feedback: Small credit union loans usually cost far less than payday loans.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Fees as a cost of borrowing
questions.question: Why are payday loans easy to get but costly?

choices.text: They are free for all first-time borrowers in every state
The government pays the fees
They require little checking but charge very high fees
They lower your other bills

questions.correct_answer: They require little checking but charge very high fees
questions.feedback: Easy approval comes with very high fees that can trap borrowers in repeat loans.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Comparing high-cost options with safer ones
questions.intro: Comparing the dollar cost of each option over the same time shows how much a lower APR saves.
questions.question: Option 1: payday loan, $45 fee for $300 for 2 weeks. Option 2: credit union small loan, $300 at 28% APR for 2 weeks (simple interest). About how much does Option 2 cost?
questions.feedback: $300 × 0.28 × (14 ÷ 365) ≈ $3.22, compared with a $45 payday fee.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Comparing high-cost options with safer ones
questions.intro: A pawn loan uses an item, such as jewelry, as collateral. If the loan is not repaid, the shop keeps and sells the item. Monthly fees add up quickly.
questions.question: A borrower takes a $500 pawn loan with a $60 monthly fee and repays after 3 months. What is the total cost of the loan?

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Comparing high-cost options with safer ones
questions.intro: Most payday loans cover regular expenses or small emergencies. Building even a small savings cushion breaks the cycle.
questions.question: Which question helps someone avoid needing a payday loan next time?

choices.text: Which payday lender has the nicest store?
How can I build a small emergency fund?
How can I find a lender that checks nothing?
How many payday loans can I have at once?

questions.correct_answer: How can I build a small emergency fund?
questions.feedback: Even a small fund replaces the need for high-cost credit.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Comparing high-cost options with safer ones
questions.intro: "Loan stacking" means having several buy now, pay later plans at once. Payments on different schedules are easy to forget.
questions.question: Jo has four BNPL plans with payments due on different dates. What is the main risk?

choices.text: BNPL plans always charge 30% interest on every purchase
BNPL lowers her income
BNPL is illegal in most states
Losing track and missing payments, adding fees

questions.correct_answer: Losing track and missing payments, adding fees
questions.feedback: Several plans at once make it easy to overspend and miss payments.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Comparing high-cost options with safer ones
questions.intro: With an installment loan, you own the item when you buy it and repay the lender. With rent-to-own, the store keeps ownership while you make rental payments.
questions.question: Which feature makes rent-to-own different from a regular purchase on an installment loan?

choices.text: You own the item immediately
There is no cost beyond the store's regular price
You do not own the item until the final payment
The item is always new

questions.correct_answer: You do not own the item until the final payment
questions.feedback: Miss a payment and the store can take the item back, even after many payments.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Why people use high-cost credit, and how to respond
questions.intro: Lack of savings, poor access to bank credit, and urgent bills push people toward high-cost credit. Understanding the reasons helps identify better alternatives.
questions.question: Why do many people turn to payday loans?

choices.text: They need cash quickly and lack savings or other credit
Payday loans are usually cheaper than small credit union loans
Payday loans improve credit scores
Banks require customers to use them

questions.correct_answer: They need cash quickly and lack savings or other credit
questions.feedback: Urgency and lack of alternatives drive payday borrowing.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Why people use high-cost credit, and how to respond
questions.intro: Many creditors, including utilities, offer payment plans or hardship programs. Asking costs nothing and can avoid fees.
questions.question: Ella cannot pay a $150 electric bill on time. Which step should she try BEFORE high-cost credit?

choices.text: Take a title loan on her car
Ignore the bill until it goes to collections
Take three BNPL plans for groceries
Call the utility to ask for a payment plan

questions.correct_answer: Call the utility to ask for a payment plan
questions.feedback: Creditors often have payment plans that cost far less than high-cost loans.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Why people use high-cost credit, and how to respond
questions.intro: Some employers and apps offer earned-wage access or paycheck advances for a small fee. Compare the dollar cost with other options.
questions.question: An employer offers a paycheck advance of $200 with a $5 fee, repaid from the next paycheck. Compared with a $30 payday fee, how much does it save?

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Why people use high-cost credit, and how to respond
questions.intro: States set many of the rules for payday and other small-dollar loans, including rate caps and outright bans.
questions.question: Which statement about state rules on payday loans is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Every state allows unlimited payday fees
Rules differ by state, and some ban them
Payday loans are illegal everywhere
Only the federal government sets payday rules

questions.correct_answer: Rules differ by state, and some ban them
questions.feedback: Some states cap rates or prohibit payday loans; rules vary, so check your state's regulator.

questions.set_title: High-cost credit: payday loans, title loans, rent-to-own, and buy now, pay later
questions.section_skill: Why people use high-cost credit, and how to respond
questions.intro: Unlicensed online lenders and scammers may ask for bank logins to drain accounts. Check that a lender is licensed in your state.
questions.question: Online "instant cash" sites ask for your bank login to approve a loan. What is the safest response?

choices.text: Never share bank logins with a lender
Share it to get faster approval
Share it only on weekends
Share your PIN instead of the password

questions.correct_answer: Never share bank logins with a lender
questions.feedback: Bank logins give full account access; never share them with a lender.

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) compares monthly debt payments with gross monthly income: DTI = total monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income × 100. Lenders use DTI to judge whether a borrower can handle more debt.
questions.question: Amir's gross monthly income is $4,000. His monthly debt payments are a $350 car loan, a $250 student loan, and a $100 credit card minimum. What is his debt-to-income ratio?

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: Two common payoff strategies: the avalanche method pays minimums on all debts and puts extra money toward the highest interest rate first (saving the most interest); the snowball method puts extra toward the smallest balance first (quick wins that build motivation).
questions.question: Debts: Card A $1,200 at 24% APR; Card B $400 at 18% APR; Loan C $3,000 at 7% APR. Under the AVALANCHE method, which debt gets extra payments first?

choices.text: Card B (smallest balance)
Loan C (largest balance)
Card A (highest APR)
All three equally

questions.correct_answer: Card A (highest APR)
questions.feedback: Avalanche targets the highest APR: Card A at 24%.

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: The snowball method pays minimums on all debts and puts every extra dollar toward the smallest balance first.
questions.question: Using the same three debts (Card A $1,200 at 24%; Card B $400 at 18%; Loan C $3,000 at 7%), which debt does the SNOWBALL method pay off first?

choices.text: Card A (highest APR)
Loan C (lowest APR)
Card B (smallest balance)
Loan C (largest balance)

questions.correct_answer: Card B (smallest balance)
questions.feedback: The snowball method pays the smallest balance first: Card B ($400).

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.intro: Paying down a higher-rate debt removes more interest each month: interest avoided ≈ amount × (APR ÷ 12).
questions.question: In one month, how much more interest does $200 of extra payment save on a 24% APR card than on a 7% APR loan (monthly rate = APR ÷ 12)?
questions.feedback: Card: $200 × 0.02 = $4.00. Loan: $200 × 0.07 ÷ 12 ≈ $1.17. Difference ≈ $2.83 per month, and it continues every month.

questions.section_skill: Calculate debt-to-income ratio and choose a debt repayment strategy
questions.question: A lender prefers DTI below 36%. Amir earns $4,000 gross monthly and already pays $700 in debts. What is the most in additional monthly debt payments he could take on and stay at or below 36%?

questions.intro: A ratio compares two quantities. Payments to income = payments ÷ income.
questions.question: Monthly debt payments are $500 and income is $2,500. What is the ratio of payments to income, as a fraction in simplest form?

questions.intro: To write a fraction as a percent, divide, then multiply by 100.
questions.question: Write 1/5 as a percent.

questions.intro: Lenders usually calculate DTI with gross (before-tax) monthly income.
questions.question: Which income should be used for DTI as lenders usually figure it?

choices.text: Gross monthly income
Net income after a vacation
Yearly income divided by 52
Only bonus income

questions.correct_answer: Gross monthly income
questions.feedback: DTI uses gross monthly income.

questions.intro: DTI counts payments on debts (loans, credit cards, mortgages or rent in some calculations), not everyday expenses like food.
questions.question: Which counts as a monthly DEBT payment for DTI?

choices.text: A grocery bill
A student loan payment
A monthly cell phone bill
A movie ticket

questions.correct_answer: A student loan payment
questions.feedback: Loan payments count; everyday expenses usually do not.

questions.question: If DTI goes from 15% to 40%, what has happened?

choices.text: A larger share of income now goes to debt payments
Income has doubled
Debt has been paid off, freeing up more of the income
Nothing important

questions.correct_answer: A larger share of income now goes to debt payments
questions.feedback: A higher DTI means more of each dollar is committed to debt.

questions.intro: Sometimes the highest-rate debt is also the smallest balance, so both methods choose the same first target.
questions.question: Lee has $300 a month for debts beyond minimums. Debts: $500 at 22%, $2,000 at 22%, $800 at 10%. Which method choice is the same under both avalanche and snowball for the first target?

choices.text: Both pay the $2,000 debt at 22% first
Both pay the $500 debt at 22% first
Both pay the $800 debt first
They disagree on every debt

questions.correct_answer: Both pay the $500 debt at 22% first
questions.feedback: The $500 debt is the smallest AND tied for the highest rate.

questions.intro: Research on behavior suggests quick wins can help people stick with a plan. The best method is one you will actually follow.
questions.question: Which reason might lead someone to choose the snowball method even though it can cost more interest?

choices.text: It always saves the most interest
Lenders require it
It lowers the interest rates on the other debts automatically
Paying off small debts quickly keeps them motivated

questions.correct_answer: Paying off small debts quickly keeps them motivated
questions.feedback: Motivation from early payoffs can matter as much as the math.

questions.intro: The "rollover" step: when one debt is paid off, its payment is added to the next target, so payments grow like a snowball.
questions.question: After Card B ($400) is paid off, Lee rolls its $40 minimum plus his $200 extra into the next debt. How much now goes to the next debt each month beyond its own minimum?

questions.intro: The interest saved by paying one debt instead of another is about the amount × the difference in rates.
questions.question: Two $1,000 debts: one at 25% APR, one at 5% APR. Paying the 25% debt first instead of the 5% debt avoids roughly how much interest per year on that $1,000?

questions.intro: A debt inventory, a list of every debt with its balance, rate, and minimum payment, is the starting point for any payoff plan.
questions.question: Which step should come BEFORE choosing a payoff method?

choices.text: Opening a new credit card
Skipping minimum payments on the smallest debts for a while
Listing each debt's balance, rate, and minimum
Closing all savings accounts

questions.correct_answer: Listing each debt's balance, rate, and minimum
questions.feedback: You cannot choose a target without knowing balances, rates, and minimums.

questions.intro: Debt consolidation combines several debts into one new loan, ideally at a lower rate. It can lower interest and simplify payments, but only if the new rate is lower and new debt is not added.
questions.question: Pia combines $6,000 of credit card debt at 23% APR into a personal loan at 11% APR. About how much interest does this save in the first year (simple estimate on the full balance)?

questions.intro: Consolidation moves debt; it does not change spending habits.
questions.question: After consolidating, Pia keeps using her credit cards and builds new balances. What happens?

choices.text: The loan pays the new card debt automatically
Her rate on the cards drops to 11%
Her total debt goes down
She ends up with the loan AND new card debt

questions.correct_answer: She ends up with the loan AND new card debt
questions.feedback: Without changing spending, consolidation can lead to more total debt.

questions.intro: An origination fee is a one-time charge for making a loan, often a percent of the loan amount. It adds to the cost and should be included in comparisons.
questions.question: A consolidation loan has a 5% origination fee on $6,000. How much is the fee?

questions.intro: Debt relief companies that sell services by phone generally cannot charge fees until they actually settle or reduce a debt. Up-front fee demands are a warning sign.
questions.question: Which consolidation offer should raise suspicion?

choices.text: A credit union loan with a stated APR and no prepayment penalty
A bank personal loan with a clear fee schedule
A company that wants large fees up front to "settle" debts
A nonprofit credit counselor offering a free budget review

questions.correct_answer: A company that wants large fees up front to "settle" debts
questions.feedback: Up-front fees for debt settlement are a red flag.

questions.intro: Nonprofit credit counseling agencies can review your budget and debts and may offer debt management plans.
questions.question: Where can someone get free or low-cost help making a debt plan?

choices.text: A nonprofit credit counseling agency
A payday lender
An anonymous social media account offering tips
A rent-to-own store

questions.correct_answer: A nonprofit credit counseling agency
questions.feedback: Reputable nonprofit credit counselors help with budgets and debt plans.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Missing a payment usually brings a late fee first. Payments 30 or more days late can be reported to credit bureaus and hurt credit scores. Unpaid debts can be sold to collectors, and creditors can sue for unpaid debts.
questions.question: Ana misses a credit card payment by 10 days. Which consequence is MOST likely first?

choices.text: Immediate arrest
A late fee
Her wages are garnished the next day
Her bank account is closed by law

questions.correct_answer: A late fee

misconceptions.D: Not a consequence of a late card payment

questions.feedback: A late fee usually comes first; credit reporting generally follows when a payment is 30+ days late.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Under federal law, most negative items stay on credit reports for 7 years. Some bankruptcies can stay for up to 10 years. Positive information can stay longer.
questions.question: Most negative information, such as late payments or collections, can stay on a credit report for about how long?

choices.text: 7 months
7 years
30 days
Forever

questions.correct_answer: 7 years
questions.feedback: About 7 years for most negative items; up to 10 years for some bankruptcies.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act gives consumers rights: collectors must provide validation information about the debt, consumers can dispute it, and collectors may not harass, threaten, or lie.
questions.question: A debt collector calls about an old debt Sam does not recognize. What right does he have?

choices.text: To have the whole debt erased simply by asking for that
To make the collector pay him for the call
None; collectors can say anything
To dispute the debt and receive validation information

questions.correct_answer: To dispute the debt and receive validation information
questions.feedback: He can dispute the debt; the collector must provide information validating it.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Collectors may not threaten arrest or legal action they cannot or do not intend to take.
questions.question: A collector threatens to have Rina arrested over a $400 credit card debt. What is true?

choices.text: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
She must pay immediately or go to jail
Collectors may say anything to get paid
Arrest is a normal step for unpaid debts over $300

questions.correct_answer: This threat is illegal; debt is not a crime
questions.feedback: Threatening arrest for ordinary debt is a prohibited practice. She can report it to the CFPB.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Explain the consequences of missed payments and the rights of consumers with debt in collection
questions.intro: Bankruptcy is a federal court process. Chapter 7 can discharge many debts, sometimes after selling some assets; Chapter 13 sets a repayment plan, usually over 3–5 years. Some debts, such as most student loans and child support, are hard or impossible to discharge.
questions.question: What is bankruptcy?

choices.text: A free way to cancel all debts with no consequences
A type of savings account
A court process to erase or reorganize debts
A credit card for people with debt

questions.correct_answer: A court process to erase or reorganize debts
questions.feedback: Bankruptcy is a serious legal option of last resort with lasting credit effects.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: A due date is the deadline for a payment. Paying after it can bring a late fee and, if very late, other consequences.
questions.question: A bill says "Due June 15." Ali pays on June 18. What usually happens?

choices.text: He may be charged a late fee
Nothing, because three days is close enough
The bill is cancelled
He earns interest

questions.correct_answer: He may be charged a late fee
questions.feedback: Paying after the due date can trigger a late fee.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.section_skill: Due dates, late fees, and minimum payments
questions.intro: The minimum payment is the smallest amount that keeps an account in good standing that month. It does not pay off the balance.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: Consumers can tell a debt collector in writing to stop contacting them. The collector may then contact them only to confirm or to say it will take a specific action, such as filing a lawsuit. The debt itself still exists.

questions.set_title: When debt goes wrong: late payments, collections, and bankruptcy
questions.intro: After a collector first contacts you, it must send validation information. If you dispute the debt in writing within the validation period (generally 30 days), the collector must pause collection until it verifies the debt.

30 days
1 year

Calling during normal hours to ask for payment

A classmate who asks
A social media follower

A record of school grades
A bank's advertisement history

Saving money in a piggy bank

questions.feedback: Hard inquiries come from credit applications.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Soft inquiries, including checking your own credit, do not affect credit scores.
questions.question: Which inquiry does NOT affect a credit score?

choices.text: Applying for a car loan
Checking your own credit report
Applying for a credit card
Applying for a private student loan

questions.correct_answer: Checking your own credit report
questions.feedback: Checking your own credit is a soft inquiry with no score impact.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Paying a collection usually updates its status to "paid," but the record can remain for the reporting period allowed by law.
questions.question: A report shows a collection account that Ana paid in full 2 years ago. What should it show now?

choices.text: Nothing; paid collections vanish immediately
A new unpaid collection
The collection, updated to show it was paid
A higher balance

questions.correct_answer: The collection, updated to show it was paid
questions.feedback: It should be updated as paid; it may remain on the report for the allowed time.

questions.section_skill: Reading a credit report line by line
questions.intro: Lenders choose which bureaus to report to, and reporting dates differ, so the three reports may not match exactly.
questions.question: Ana reviews her reports from all three bureaus. Why might they differ?

choices.text: One of them must be fake
Not every lender reports to every bureau
Bureaus copy each other's reports exactly every day
Reports are random

questions.correct_answer: Not every lender reports to every bureau
questions.feedback: Different reporting leads to differences; check all three.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: A credit freeze (security freeze) restricts access to your credit report, so identity thieves cannot easily open new accounts in your name. Freezes are free at each bureau, and you can lift them temporarily when you apply for credit.
questions.question: What does a credit freeze do?

choices.text: It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
It lowers your credit score
It closes your existing cards
It stops you from using your own debit card or checks

questions.correct_answer: It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
questions.feedback: A freeze blocks most new-credit checks without affecting your score or existing accounts.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: Since 2018, federal law has required the nationwide credit bureaus to place and lift credit freezes for free.
questions.question: How much does it cost to place a credit freeze at a nationwide bureau?

choices.text: $10 per bureau each year
$100 one time
A fee of 1% of your total credit limit
Nothing; freezes are free by law

questions.correct_answer: Nothing; freezes are free by law
questions.feedback: Freezes are free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: You can lift a freeze temporarily for a specific time or lender, then it returns.
questions.question: Ana froze her credit and now wants to apply for a car loan. What should she do?

choices.text: Lift the freeze for a short time
Delete her credit history
Apply under a friend's name
Nothing; lenders can see frozen reports

questions.correct_answer: Lift the freeze for a short time
questions.feedback: A temporary lift lets the lender check her credit.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.intro: A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening credit. A credit freeze blocks most access to your report.
questions.question: How is a fraud alert different from a credit freeze?

choices.text: An alert closes your accounts
A freeze costs money; an alert is free
They are identical; both close your current accounts
An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access

questions.correct_answer: An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access
questions.feedback: Alerts add verification; freezes restrict access.

questions.section_skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection
questions.question: Which teen habit best protects future credit?

choices.text: Posting a full birth date and address online
Keeping a Social Security number private
Sharing passwords with friends
Using the same password everywhere

questions.correct_answer: Keeping a Social Security number private
questions.feedback: Protecting your SSN and personal data prevents thieves from opening accounts in your name.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: A credit score is a number (often 300–850) that summarizes credit risk based on a credit report. FICO's general weights: payment history about 35%, amounts owed about 30%, length of credit history about 15%, new credit about 10%, and credit mix about 10%. Other scoring models exist.
questions.question: In the widely used FICO model, which factor has the LARGEST weight?

choices.text: Credit mix (about 10%)
New credit (about 10%)
Payment history (about 35%)
Length of credit history (about 15%)

questions.correct_answer: Payment history (about 35%)
questions.feedback: Paying on time matters most.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Credit scores affect the interest rates lenders offer. A higher score usually means a lower rate, which lowers monthly payments and total cost.
questions.question: Two applicants want a $20,000, 5-year car loan. Applicant A (strong credit) is offered 6% APR, with a $386.66 payment; Applicant B is offered 12% APR, with a $444.89 payment. How much more does B pay over 5 years?

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Scores reward on-time payments and low balances compared with limits, and can drop with late payments, high balances, and many new applications.
questions.question: Which action is MOST likely to raise a credit score over time?

choices.text: Opening several new cards in one month
Maxing out a credit card
Paying every bill on time
Closing your oldest account

questions.correct_answer: Paying every bill on time
questions.feedback: Consistent on-time payments are the strongest positive factor.

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.intro: Credit scores use only information in credit reports. Income, employment, savings, age, race, and where you live are not part of the score.
questions.question: Which is NOT used in calculating FICO credit scores?

choices.text: Payment history
Income
Amounts owed
Length of credit history

questions.correct_answer: Income
questions.feedback: Income is not in credit reports, so it is not in the score (lenders may still ask about it).

questions.section_skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs
questions.question: Ivy's FICO score is 780; Max's is 580. Which statement is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Max will pay lower rates, since lower is better
Both will get identical offers
Scores do not affect borrowing
Max will likely face higher rates or denials

questions.correct_answer: Max will likely face higher rates or denials
questions.feedback: On the 300–850 scale, higher scores indicate lower risk and usually get better terms.

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.intro: Parts of a whole are added to find a combined share.
questions.question: If payment history is 35% of a score and amounts owed is 30%, together they make up what percent?

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.intro: Percents of the same whole can be compared directly.
questions.question: Which is larger: 15% or 10%?

choices.text: They are equal
It cannot be compared

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.question: Five factors weigh 35%, 30%, 15%, 10%, and 10%. What is their total?
questions.feedback: They add to 100%: the whole score model.

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.question: A score went from 650 to 700. By how many points did it rise?

questions.section_skill: Percent weights and parts of a whole
questions.intro: Length of credit history considers how long your accounts have been open, on average and for the oldest account.
questions.question: Which factor relates to how long accounts have been open?

choices.text: Length of credit history
Payment history
Amounts owed
Credit mix

questions.correct_answer: Length of credit history
questions.feedback: Length of credit history measures account age.

questions.intro: Landlords often review credit reports or scores because past bill-paying predicts rent payment.
questions.question: A landlord checks Tia's credit before approving an apartment. Why?

choices.text: To see her school grades
To predict whether she will pay rent on time
To check her medical history and recent doctor visits
To learn her income

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
questions.feedback: Credit history helps landlords predict on-time rent.

questions.intro: Many insurers use credit-based insurance scores to help set prices, where state law allows.
questions.question: In many states, auto insurers use credit-based insurance scores. What does this mean for drivers with weaker credit?

choices.text: They pay lower premiums
They cannot buy insurance
They may pay higher premiums
Their driving record is ignored

questions.correct_answer: They may pay higher premiums
questions.feedback: Weaker credit can raise premiums in states that allow this.

questions.intro: Employers may review credit reports (not scores) for some jobs, but federal law requires your written permission. Some states limit this further.
questions.question: An employer wants to check Tia's credit report for a job. What must happen first?

choices.text: Nothing; employers can check anyone
Tia must pay a fee
The employer must lend Tia money
Tia must give written permission

questions.correct_answer: Tia must give written permission
questions.feedback: Written permission is required for employment checks.

questions.intro: Over long loans, a small rate difference adds up: extra cost = monthly difference × number of payments.
questions.question: A 100-point lower score raises a $250,000 mortgage rate from 6.5% to 7.5%. Payments rise from $1,580 to $1,748 a month. How much more is paid over 30 years?

questions.intro: FICO and VantageScore both make several versions, and each bureau's data differs, so scores vary.
questions.question: Which statement about "credit scores" is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Everyone has one official score set by the government
Scores never change
Different models give a person many scores
Scores are the same at every bureau

questions.correct_answer: Different models give a person many scores
questions.feedback: Different models and bureaus produce different scores.

questions.intro: Checking your own report or score is a soft inquiry and never affects scores.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Checking my own credit report lowers my score."

choices.text: Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
Fact: every check lowers your score
Fact: only on weekends
Fact: each check lowers your score by about 50 points

questions.correct_answer: Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
questions.feedback: Self-checks are soft inquiries; check as often as you like.

questions.intro: Card use is reported each month. Paying the full statement balance shows responsible use without paying interest.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Carrying a small balance and paying interest helps your score."

choices.text: Fact: interest payments raise scores
Myth: paying in full still shows on-time use
Fact: only balances over $1,000 count toward building credit
Fact: scores need debt to exist

questions.correct_answer: Myth: paying in full still shows on-time use
questions.feedback: You do not need to pay interest to build credit.

questions.intro: Credit scores use only information in credit reports.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "My income determines my credit score."

choices.text: Fact: higher income always means a higher score
Fact: scores are a percent of income
Fact: only salaried workers have scores
Myth: income is not in credit reports

questions.correct_answer: Myth: income is not in credit reports
questions.feedback: Income is not part of the score, though lenders consider it separately.

questions.intro: Closing a card removes its credit limit from your total available credit and may eventually shorten your credit history.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Closing an old, unused card always raises my score."

choices.text: Fact: fewer cards always means higher scores
Fact: closed cards are deleted immediately
Myth: it can raise utilization and shorten history
Fact: closing a card erases its late payments from your report

questions.correct_answer: Myth: it can raise utilization and shorten history
questions.feedback: Closing a card can raise your utilization ratio and, over time, shorten your history.

questions.intro: Scoring models usually treat multiple inquiries for the same kind of loan (car, mortgage, student) within a short window as one, so you can shop for the best rate.
questions.question: Myth or fact: "Shopping for a car loan at several lenders within a short period ruins my score."

choices.text: Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
Fact: each inquiry costs about 50 points every time
Fact: you must never compare lenders
Fact: only the first lender counts

questions.correct_answer: Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
questions.feedback: Rate shopping within a short window is generally treated as a single inquiry.

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: Credit utilization = card balances ÷ credit limits × 100. It is a major part of the "amounts owed" score factor. Lower utilization generally helps scores; a common guideline is to stay below about 30%, and lower is better.
questions.question: Tia's card has a $1,500 limit, and her statement balance is $450. What is her credit utilization?

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: Overall utilization adds all balances and divides by all limits.
questions.question: Max has two cards: $300 balance on a $1,000 limit and $700 on a $2,500 limit. What is his overall utilization (nearest tenth)?

misconceptions.C: Divides by the larger limit only

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: Starter options include a secured credit card (you put down a deposit that usually becomes your limit), a credit-builder loan (payments are saved for you and released at the end), and being added as an authorized user on a parent's card. Paying on time builds history.
questions.question: Leo has no credit history. Which product is designed to help someone start building credit?

choices.text: A payday loan
A prepaid debit card
A savings account that comes with no card attached
A secured credit card backed by a cash deposit

questions.correct_answer: A secured credit card backed by a cash deposit

misconceptions.A: Usually not reported and very costly

questions.feedback: A secured card reports like a regular card but is backed by a deposit.

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.intro: An authorized user can use someone else's card. Many issuers report the account to the authorized user's credit file too, which can help, or hurt if the account is misused.
questions.question: Leo is added as an authorized user on his mother's card. Her account has a long on-time history and low utilization. What can this do?

choices.text: Make Leo responsible for her past debts
Help Leo's credit file show positive history
Give Leo his own separate credit limit and account
Erase his mother's late payments

questions.correct_answer: Help Leo's credit file show positive history
questions.feedback: The account's positive history may appear on Leo's report.

questions.section_skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products
questions.question: Which plan builds credit with the LEAST cost?

choices.text: Carry a balance each month to show activity
Max out the card, then pay the minimum
Charge a small bill and pay it in full
Never use the card at all

questions.correct_answer: Charge a small bill and pay it in full
questions.feedback: Small, regular use paid in full builds history without interest.

questions.intro: Percent = part ÷ whole × 100.
questions.question: $200 is what percent of $1,000?

questions.intro: Part = percent × whole.
questions.question: A card has a $2,000 limit. What balance equals 10% utilization?
Which utilization is LOWEST?

choices.text: $100 of a $500 limit
$100 of a $2,000 limit
$400 of a $1,000 limit
$900 of a $3,000 limit

questions.correct_answer: $100 of a $2,000 limit

questions.intro: Utilization is balance ÷ limit. A larger limit with the same balance makes the fraction smaller.
questions.question: If balances stay the same and a credit limit increases, what happens to utilization?

choices.text: It goes up
It stays the same
It becomes 100%
It goes down

questions.correct_answer: It goes down
questions.feedback: A larger denominator lowers the percent.

questions.question: A card with a $500 limit has a $500 balance. What is utilization?

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: With a credit-builder loan, the lender holds the loan amount in an account while you make payments. Payments are reported to bureaus, and you receive the money at the end. The cost is the interest and fees.
questions.question: A credit-builder loan of $600 is held in a savings account while Ana makes 12 payments of $52. What does she receive at the end, and what did it cost?
questions.feedback: 12 × $52 = $624 paid; she receives $600; cost $24.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: A secured card works like a regular credit card for utilization: balance ÷ limit.
questions.question: Leo opens a secured card with a $300 deposit and a $300 limit. He charges $30 a month and pays in full. What is his utilization each month?

misconceptions.C: Uses the deposit as a percent

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: Many secured cards review accounts after a period of good use and may convert them to regular (unsecured) cards.
questions.question: After a year of on-time payments, some issuers "graduate" a secured card. What usually happens?

choices.text: The deposit is kept as a fee
The card is closed and a penalty is charged to Leo
It becomes a regular card; the deposit is returned
Leo must pay a new deposit

questions.correct_answer: It becomes a regular card; the deposit is returned
questions.feedback: Graduation returns the deposit and keeps the account history.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: A secured card helps build credit only if the issuer reports your payments to the credit bureaus.
questions.question: Which question should Leo ask before opening a secured card?

choices.text: Does the issuer report to all three credit bureaus?
Does the card have a cool design?
Can I use the card to get payday loans more easily?
Will it let me skip payments?

questions.correct_answer: Does the issuer report to all three credit bureaus?
questions.feedback: Reporting to the bureaus is what builds credit.

questions.section_skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail
questions.intro: When you pay the full balance every month, the APR does not affect your cost, but annual fees do.
questions.question: A secured card has a $49 annual fee and 25.99% APR; another has $0 fee and 28.99% APR. Leo will pay in full every month. Which is cheaper?

choices.text: The $49-fee card, because its APR is lower
The $0-fee card
They cost the same
Neither; both charge $49

questions.correct_answer: The $0-fee card

misconceptions.A: APR does not matter if paid in full

questions.feedback: Paying in full means no interest, so the annual fee is the only cost.

questions.intro: The key habits for building credit are on-time payment, low balances, and few new applications.
questions.question: Which step comes FIRST in a safe credit-building plan for a student?

choices.text: Apply for five cards at once
Spend up to the limit each month to show activity
Lend the card to friends
Set up autopay for the full statement balance

questions.correct_answer: Set up autopay for the full statement balance
questions.feedback: Autopay in full prevents late payments and interest from day one.

questions.intro: Card issuers usually report the balance shown on your statement. Paying before the statement closes lowers the reported balance and utilization.
questions.question: Tia's statement balance would be $480 on a $600 limit (80%). She pays $400 BEFORE the statement closes. What utilization is reported?

choices.text: About 13%

questions.correct_answer: About 13%

questions.intro: Late payments of 30 days or more are usually reported to the bureaus and can stay on a credit report for years.
questions.question: Which habit could LOWER Tia's score during her first year?

choices.text: Paying in full each month
Missing a payment by 30+ days
Keeping utilization under 10%
Checking her own credit report

questions.correct_answer: Missing a payment by 30+ days
questions.feedback: A 30-day late payment is reported and can hurt a score for years.

questions.intro: Utilization = balance ÷ limit.
questions.question: After a year, Tia's issuer offers a higher limit with no fee. If her spending stays the same, what effect does accepting it usually have?

choices.text: Lower utilization
Higher utilization
A new late payment
A closed account

questions.correct_answer: Lower utilization
questions.feedback: The same balance on a larger limit is a smaller percent, as long as spending does not rise.

questions.question: Which is the BEST way to check progress on building credit?

choices.text: Pay for a "score boost" service
Ask friends what their scores are
Check free reports and scores regularly
Apply for loans now and then to see if approved

questions.correct_answer: Check free reports and scores regularly
questions.feedback: Free reports and scores show progress without cost or inquiries.
